relevance_reason: Reports novel MPZ mutations in patients with congenital hypomyelination, which links MPZ to this CHN2 entry. Only the abstract is available, so no variant details are given.

findings.statement: Warner et al. (1996) identified 5 novel mutations in the MPZ gene, which encodes the major structural protein (P0) of peripheral nerve myelin, in patients with Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1B, Dejerine-Sottas syndrome, or congenital hypomyelination.
quotes: We have identified five novel mutations in the myelin protein zero (MPZ) gene, encoding the major structural protein (P0) of peripheral nerve myelin, in patients with either CMT1B, DSS, or CH.

findings.statement: Warner et al. (1996) suggested that CMT1B, Dejerine-Sottas syndrome, and congenital hypomyelination may not be distinct pathophysiologic entities. Instead, they proposed that these disorders form a spectrum of related 'myelinopathies' caused by an underlying defect in myelination.
quotes: This finding suggests that these disorders may not be distinct pathophysiologic entities, but rather represent a spectrum of related "myelinopathies" due to an underlying defect in myelination.

findings.statement: Warner et al. (1996) hypothesized that the differences in clinical severity seen with MPZ mutations depend on the type of mutation and its effect on protein function, that is, loss of function versus a dominant-negative effect.
quotes: we hypothesize the differences in clinical severity seen with mutations in MPZ are related to the type of mutation and its subsequent effect on protein function (i.e., loss of function versus dominant negative).

relevance_reason: Only the title is available. It describes an ultrastructural nerve biopsy study of one case of early infantile chronic neuropathy, which is an early clinicopathologic report relevant to congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. No genetic data are given.

findings.statement: Lyon (1969) reported an ultrastructural (electron microscopic) study of a nerve biopsy from a patient with early infantile chronic neuropathy.
quotes: Ultrastructural study of a nerve biopsy from a case of early infantile chronic neuropathy.

relevance_reason: Reports a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy carrying a novel MPZ mutation (Thr124Lys).

findings.statement: Kochanski et al. (2004) identified a novel Thr124Lys mutation in the MPZ gene in a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy.
quotes: The authors describe the clinical and morphologic features of a patient with CHN and the identification of a novel Thr124Lys mutation in the MPZ gene.

findings.statement: Kochanski et al. (2004) described the clinical and morphologic features of a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, a severe neuropathy with early infancy onset in which sural nerve biopsy characteristically shows nonmyelinated and poorly myelinated axons with basal lamina onion bulbs and lack of myelin breakdown products.
quotes: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy (CHN; MIM# 605253) is a severe neuropathy with early infancy onset inherited as an autosomal dominant or recessive trait.
Sural nerve biopsy shows a characteristic picture of nonmyelinated and poorly myelinated axons with basal lamina onion bulbs and lack of myelin breakdown products.

phenotypes.text: severe neuropathy with early infancy onset
poorly myelinated axons on sural nerve biopsy

relevance_reason: Reports a congenital hypomyelination patient with a de novo MPZ Q215X mutation, which directly establishes CHN2 as an MPZ-related disorder.

findings.statement: Mandich et al. (1999) described the clinical, morphologic, and immunohistochemical features of a patient with congenital hypomyelination (CH). CH is a hereditary demyelinating peripheral neuropathy with onset in early infancy, distal muscle weakness, hypotonia, areflexia, and severely slowed nerve conduction velocities. The authors noted that the patient's clinical features were quite distinct from those of CMT1B or Dejerine-Sottas syndrome.
quotes: Congenital hypomyelination (CH) is a hereditary demyelinating peripheral neuropathy characterized by early infancy onset, distal muscle weakness, hypotonia, areflexia, and severe slowing of nerve conduction velocities.
a patient presenting with clinical features quite distinct from those of the more frequent Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1B disease (CMT1B) or Dejerine-Sottas syndrome (DSS)

phenotypes.text: severe slowing of nerve conduction velocities

findings.statement: Mandich et al. (1999) identified a de novo Q215X mutation in the MPZ gene in a patient with congenital hypomyelination. The authors concluded that this confirmed CH is allelic with disorders that have a milder phenotype and a different clinical and neuropathologic profile, such as CMT1B and Dejerine-Sottas syndrome.
quotes: the identification of a mutation in the gene (MPZ) for protein zero (P0) associated with this phenotype are described
This "de novo" mutation in a patient presenting with clinical features quite distinct
confirms that CH is allelic with other disorders characterized by a less severe phenotype and a different clinical and neuropathological profile

relevance_reason: Reports a family with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy and a heterozygous MPZ mutation in two generations, followed long term.

findings.statement: Smit et al. (2008) described a family with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy in which a heterozygous mutation in the MPZ gene was confirmed in two generations.
quotes: Here we describe a family with a heterozygous mutation in MPZ, confirmed in two generations.

findings.statement: Smit et al. (2008) noted that congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy is a rare condition with prenatal, neonatal, or early infantile onset of hypotonia, paresis, and areflexia. Histopathology shows absent or thin myelin sheaths, and most of the few reported patients die within the first years of life. Mutations had been described in the MPZ, EGR2, PMP22, and MTMR2 genes.
quotes: Congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy is a rare condition characterized by prenatal, neonatal or early infantile onset of hypotonia, paresis and areflexia.
Most of the few patients described in literature die within the first years of life. Histopathologically there are no or thin myelin sheaths.
Mutations have been described in the following genes, MPZ, EGR2, PMP22, and MTMR2.

relevance_reason: Case report of a congenital hypomyelinating (amyelinating) neuropathy that presented as lethal arthrogryposis multiplex congenita, with nerve pathology and myelin protein immunocytochemistry. The abstract reports no gene or variant.

findings.statement: Charnas et al. (1988) described an infant born at 37 weeks' gestation who had lethal arthrogryposis multiplex congenita caused by complete absence of peripheral nervous system myelin. Supernumerary Schwann cells (onion bulbs) were not found.
quotes: We describe a 37-week gestational age infant who presented with lethal arthrogryposis multiplex congenita due to complete absence of peripheral nervous system (PNS) myelin.
No supernumerary Schwann cells (onion bulbs) were found.

phenotypes.text: complete absence of peripheral nerve myelin

findings.statement: In this patient, Charnas et al. (1988) found that Schwann cells proliferated, migrated, ensheathed axons, produced basal lamina and then stopped proliferating normally, but they failed in spiral lengthening and longitudinal growth. The distance between Schwann cell nuclei was very short, giving marked Schwann cell hypercellularity, and the Schwann cells took on many morphologic features of unmyelinated nerves. Immunocytochemistry detected none of the PNS myelin proteins P0, P1 or MAG. The authors concluded that the defect appeared to be an arrest in Schwann cell differentiation at the stages of mesaxon elongation and longitudinal growth.
quotes: Schwann cells accomplished successful developmental proliferation, migration, axonal ensheathment, basal lamina production, and subsequent cessation of proliferation, but failed in spiral lengthening and longitudinal growth.
No PNS myelin proteins (P0, P1, MAG) were detected by immunocytochemical methods, and the Schwann cells adopted many morphologic features characteristic of unmyelinated nerves.
The defect appears to be an arrest in Schwann cell differentiation at the stages of mesaxon elongation and longitudinal growth.

phenotypes.text: absent P0, P1 and MAG myelin proteins

relevance_reason: The paper is a case report of congenital hypomyelination neuropathy with clinical and nerve pathology findings. It reports no molecular data.

findings.statement: Ono et al. (1982) described a 3-year 11-month-old Japanese boy with congenital hypomyelination. He had delayed motor development, generalized muscle hypotonia and weakness, and absent tendon reflexes due to peripheral neuropathy. His mental development was normal. Nerve conduction velocities could not be measured.
quotes: A 3 year, 11 month-old Japanese male with congenital hypomyelination is described.
Clinical features are delay of motor development, generalized muscle hypotonia and weakness, absent tendon reflexes due to peripheral neuropathy, and normal mental development.
Electrophysiologically, nerve conduction velocities could not be measured.

findings.statement: In the same patient, Ono et al. (1982) found on right sural nerve biopsy that most myelinated fibers had no myelin at all. Electron microscopy showed onion bulbs around the fibers, formed by concentric double-layered sheets of basement membrane with fragments of Schwann cell cytoplasm. The authors noted that these features were similar to previously reported cases.
quotes: Histological examination of the right sural nerve revealed total of absence myelin of most of the myelinated fibers.
there was a concentric network of lamellae formed by double-layered sheets of basement membranes with fragments of Schwann cell cytoplasm around the myelinated fibers, so called "onion-bulbs".

phenotypes.text: absence of myelin in most myelinated fibers of the sural nerve

relevance_reason: Reports a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy who carries an MPZ point mutation, plus long-term clinical follow-up.

findings.statement: Phillips et al. (1999) reported long-term prospective follow-up of 2 unrelated girls with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. The first presented with neonatal hypotonia and extremely slow nerve conduction velocities, and sural nerve biopsy showed profound hypomyelination without inflammation or myelin breakdown. At age 9 years her motor function was still improving, but follow-up nerve conduction velocities had not changed.
quotes: The authors report the long-term prospective follow-up of two unrelated females with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy (CHN) and review previously reported cases.

The authors' first patient presented with neonatal hypotonia and extremely slow nerve conduction velocities. Sural nerve biopsy revealed profound hypomyelination, without inflammation or evidence of myelin breakdown.
She is now 9 years of age, and her motor function has continued to improve. Follow-up nerve-conduction velocities are unchanged.

phenotypes.text: profound hypomyelination on sural nerve biopsy
no inflammation or myelin breakdown on nerve biopsy

findings.statement: Phillips et al. (1999) described a second girl with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy who presented with hypotonia at age 5 months. Her nerve conduction velocities were extremely slow, and sural nerve biopsy showed severe hypomyelination without inflammation or myelin breakdown. At age 5 years her motor function had improved, but repeat nerve conduction velocities had not changed. Both patients had normal cognitive development.
quotes: The authors' second patient presented at 5 months with hypotonia. Nerve-conduction velocities were extremely slow, and sural nerve biopsy revealed severe hypomyelination, with no inflammation or evidence of myelin breakdown.
She is now 5 years of age and has also demonstrated improved motor function. Repeated nerve-conduction velocities are unchanged. Both patients have normal cognitive development.

phenotypes.text: severe hypomyelination on sural nerve biopsy

findings.statement: Phillips et al. (1999) found a point mutation in the myelin protein zero gene (MPZ) in their second patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy. The same mutation had been reported in 3 other patients diagnosed with Dejerine-Sottas syndrome but never in a patient with CHN. The authors suggested that CHN, although a distinct clinical entity, may share similar genetic features with DSS.
quotes: Molecular genetic analysis in Patient 2 disclosed a point mutation in the myelin protein zero gene; this same point mutation has been reported in three other patients diagnosed with Dejerine-Sottas syndrome (DSS) but has never been reported in a patient with CHN.
Although CHN is a distinct clinical entity, it may share similar genetic features with DSS.

variants.as_reported: point mutation in the myelin protein zero gene

relevance_reason: Case report of congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy caused by a de novo MPZ frameshift mutation.

findings.statement: Szigeti et al. (2003) reported a patient with congenital hypomyelination associated with cranial nerve dysfunction, respiratory failure, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, the last confounding the clinical picture. Muscle biopsy findings suggested an effect of abnormal innervation on early postnatal muscle fiber differentiation.
quotes: We report a case of congenital hypomyelination associated with cranial nerve dysfunction, respiratory failure, and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy confounding the clinical picture.
Muscle biopsy findings are presented that allude to the effect of abnormal innervation on early postnatal muscle differentiation.

phenotypes.text: disturbed muscle fiber differentiation on biopsy

findings.statement: In a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, Szigeti et al. (2003) identified a complex de novo mutation in the MPZ gene consisting of a 3-bp deletion of CTA from nucleotides 550 to 552 and insertion of G at nucleotide 550, predicted by conceptual translation to result in a frameshift.
quotes: Molecular genetic testing showed a complex de novo myelin protein zero (MPZ) mutation consisting of a 3bp deletion of CTA from nucleotide 550 to 552 and insertion of G at nucleotide 550 that by conceptual translation results in a frameshift mutation.

variants.as_reported: 3bp deletion of CTA from nucleotide 550 to 552 and insertion of G at nucleotide 550

relevance_reason: Reports a patient whose sural nerve pathology matched congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy and who carried a de novo frameshift insertion in MPZ.

findings.statement: Tachi et al. (1998) described a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype. Sural nerve biopsy showed hypomyelinated fibers without active demyelination, and onion-bulb formations made of two parallel layers of basement membrane. This pathology was consistent with congenital hypomyelination neuropathy (CHN), but his clinical features were more severe than those of previously reported CHN patients.
quotes: We present a male patient with Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype, who had a small direct tandem duplication of the Po gene.

The pathology of the sural nerve showed hypomyelinated fibers with absence of active demyelination and onion-bulb formations composed of two parallel layers of basement membrane, consistent with congenital hypomyelination neuropathy (CHN).
However, his clinical features were more severe than those of previously reported CHN patients.

phenotypes.text: hypomyelinated fibers on sural nerve biopsy

findings.statement: In a male patient with a Dejerine-Sottas disease phenotype and nerve pathology consistent with CHN, Tachi et al. (1998) identified a GGCA insertion at nucleotide 560 of the MPZ (Po) gene. The insertion was a small direct tandem duplication in exon 4, which encodes the transmembrane domain. It shifted the reading frame and created a stop codon. The mutation was not found in either parent, and the authors suggested that mutation of the transmembrane domain probably has the largest impact on Po function.
quotes: A GGCA insertion was identified at the position of nucleotide 560 in the myelin protein zero (Po) gene.
This insertional mutation was located in exon 4 coding for the transmembrane domain of the Po gene and caused a shift of reading frame, creating a stop codon.
The mutation was not identified in both parents.

relevance_reason: Transgenic mouse study showing that Mpz (P0) overexpression causes congenital hypomyelination of peripheral nerves; the authors note the resemblance to human congenital hypomyelination neuropathy and propose MPZ overexpression as a novel mechanism of hereditary neuropathy.

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) generated transgenic mice carrying extra copies of the myelin protein zero gene (Mpz) and found that they manifested a dose-dependent dysmyelinating neuropathy ranging from transient perinatal hypomyelination to arrested myelination with impaired sorting of axons by Schwann cells; Mpz mRNA overexpression ranged from 30 to 700%.
quotes: Transgenic mice containing extra copies of Mpz manifested a dose-dependent, dysmyelinating neuropathy, ranging from transient perinatal hypomyelination to arrested myelination and impaired sorting of axons by Schwann cells.
Mpz mRNA overexpression ranged from 30-700%, whereas an increased level of P(0) protein was detected only in nerves of low copy-number animals.

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) obtained ten transgenic founders with Mpz copy numbers ranging from 1 to more than 40; high copy number animals (F80.1, F80.8, F80.9, Tg80.2; copy number greater than 20) showed gait difficulty, reduced weight, tremor, atrophy of the paraspinal and hindlimb musculature and reduced life-span, with nerve conduction velocities profoundly reduced to about 2 m/s and temporal dispersion of the compound motor action potential, while leg muscles showed angulated and atrophic fibers suggestive of denervation without fiber type grouping.
quotes: F80.1, F80.8, F80.9, and Tg80.2 animals (all copy number >20) showed a severe phenotype including gait difficulty, reduced weight, tremor, atrophy of the paraspinal and hindlimb musculature (Fig. 2 A), and reduced life-span (Table).
Nerve conduction velocities in the Tg80.2 animals were profoundly reduced to ∼2 m/s with temporal dispersion of the compound motor action potential (Fig. 2 B) suggesting a dysmyelinating neuropathy.
Morphological analysis of leg muscles showed angulated and atrophic fibers suggestive of denervation, but no fiber type grouping to suggest nerve regeneration.

phenotypes.text: atrophy of paraspinal and hindlimb musculature

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) showed by semi-thin section and electron microscopic analysis of P28 sciatic nerve from high copy number Tg80.2 mice remarkable hypomyelination with an increased number of Schwann cell nuclei, no onion bulbs, bundles of unsorted naked axons of mixed caliber in every transverse section, Schwann cells surrounded by pockets of redundant basal lamina containing collagen, and little evidence of active demyelination or axonal degeneration.
quotes: Semi-thin section analysis of P28 sciatic nerve from Tg80.2 animals showed remarkable hypomyelination and an increase in the number of Schwann cell nuclei (Fig. 3).
There was little evidence of active demyelination as myelin debris was not seen extracellularly or in macrophages.
Remarkably, in each transverse section of sciatic nerve at P28, several families of Schwann cells associated with bundles of naked axons of mixed caliber were identified (Fig. 3 C, arrows).

phenotypes.text: increased number of Schwann cell nuclei

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) concluded that the dysmyelination resulted from developmental delay rather than myelin destruction: Tg80.2 sciatic nerves contained virtually no myelin at P5 and P14, fewer than 1% of axons in a 1:1 relationship with Schwann cells were myelinated in the P10 quadriceps nerve versus virtually 100% in wild type, and the motor branch was more dysmyelinated than the sensory branch of the femoral nerve.
quotes: In contrast to controls, Tg80.2 sciatic nerves at P5 and P14 contained virtually no myelin (Fig. 5).
By P10, <1% of axons in 1:1 relationships with Schwann cells were myelinated in Tg80.2 nerve, whereas virtually 100% of such axons were myelinated in wild-type nerve (Table).
Consistent with this idea, the motor branch (quadriceps) was more dysmyelinated than the sensory branch (saphenous) of femoral nerve by P10 in Tg80.2 animals (Table).

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) demonstrated that severity of dysmyelination paralleled Mpz dosage: mice with 0-10 copies (Tg80.3, 0.3-fold overexpression) were behaviorally normal with normally myelinated nerves at P28, mice with 10-20 copies (Tg80.4, 0.8-fold) had mild tremor, a nerve conduction velocity of 11 m/s and about 50% of large axons unmyelinated, and mice with more than 20 copies (Tg80.2, 7.3-fold) had evident tremor, weak grip strength, conduction velocity of 2 m/s and severe hypomyelination with delayed axonal sorting.
quotes: For example, animals with 0–10 copies (Tg80.3, F80.10) appeared behaviorally normal, and had normally myelinated nerves by P28 (Fig. 6 B). In contrast, animals with 10–20 copies (Tg80.4 and F80.7) manifested mild tremor, NCV of 11m/s (Tg80.4), and dysmyelination with ∼50% of the large axons ensheathed by single Schwann cells that had not formed myelin (Fig. 6 C).

Finally, animals with >20 copies (Tg80.2, F80.1, F80.8, and F80.9) manifested evident tremor, weak grip strength, conduction velocity of 2 m/s (Tg80.2), and severe hypomyelination along with delayed axonal sorting (Fig. 6E and Fig. F).

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) placed the threshold for dysmyelination between 30 and 80% Mpz overexpression (130-180% total Mpz expression) by breeding the mildly affected Tg80.3 line to homozygosity, which raised overexpression from 30% to 80% and produced tremor and dysmyelination, and by crossing Tg80.4 into the homozygous Mpz null background, in which myelination returned to essentially normal, showing that the phenotype depended uniquely on Mpz dosage rather than on an ectopic effect or structural alteration of the transgenic P0.
quotes: P28 Tg80.3 homozygotes manifested tremor and dysmyelination (Fig. 6 D), whereas P28 80.3 hemizygotes did not (Fig. 6 B). RT-PCR analysis confirmed an increase in overexpression from 30% in Tg80.3 hemizygote nerves to 80% in Tg80.3 homozygote nerves (Fig. 7 C).
These data demonstrate that a threshold exists for Mpz overexpression between 30 and 80% (130–180% total Mpz expression), above which dysmyelination results.
Therefore, the overexpression phenotype depends uniquely on dosage of Mpz, not on an ectopic effect or structural alteration of transgenic P0.

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) found by Western blot analysis that P0 overexpression dysregulated other myelin proteins even in the absence of dysmyelination: in P28 Tg80.3 nerves with ultrastructurally normal myelin, P0 was overexpressed by about 60% while MBP was reduced by about 50% and PMP22 by 35%, with tubulin unchanged; they concluded that Schwann cells sense and respond to P0 overexpression by dysregulating other myelin proteins before exceeding the threshold for dysmyelination.
quotes: Surprisingly, the MBP level was reduced by ∼50% in P28 Tg80.3 sciatic nerves as compared with control (Fig. 9; 0.52 ± 0.05, n = 5), in the absence of myelin abnormality (Fig. 6 B). PMP22 was also reduced by 35% in Tg80.3 (0.37 ± 0.16, n =2)
Thus, Schwann cells sense and respond to P0 overexpression by dysregulating other myelin proteins before exceeding a threshold for dysmyelination.

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) noted that the profoundly reduced nerve conduction velocities (1-2 m/s), the paucity of active myelin destruction or onion bulbs, and the redundant basement membrane formation in the P0 overexpressor mice resembled human congenital hypomyelination neuropathy (CHN), and that low-level P0 overexpression produced transient hypomyelination similar to a subset of reversible CHN; they suggested that P0 overexpression represents a new mechanism of hereditary neuropathy and that MPZ overexpression might contribute to the pathogenesis of the EGR2 mutation that likely disinhibits Krox 20.
quotes: Of note, profoundly reduced nerve conduction velocities (1–2 m/s), the paucity of active myelin destruction or onion bulbs, and the redundant basement membrane formation (Fig. 4 C) in P0 overexpressor mice resemble CHN (Harati and Butler 1985). In addition, low level P0 overexpression produces transient hypomyelination in mice, similar to a subset of reversible CHN (Ghamdi et al. 1997; Levy et al. 1997).

Since one of these EGR2 mutations likely disinhibits Krox 20 (Warner et al. 1998), and Krox 20 may regulate P0 expression (Topilko et al. 1994; Zorick et al. 1999), it is possible that MPZ overexpression contributes to the pathogenesis of this EGR2 mutation.

These studies reveal new stages in nerve development at which Schwann cells are susceptible to altered gene dosage and suggest that P0 overexpression represents a new mechanism of hereditary neuropathy.

findings.statement: Wrabetz et al. (2000) advised caution regarding replacement gene therapy for CMT1B neuropathies in which the MPZ mutation predicts loss of P0 expression, noting that such therapy may require exceptionally precise regulation of P0 expression in human nerve because only 60% overexpression in mice resulted in impaired myelin formation.
quotes: The present study advises caution for treatment of CMT1B neuropathies in which the MPZ mutation predicts loss of P0 expression, and for which replacement gene therapy might therefore be considered (Shy et al. 1995; Guenard et al. 1999). Such therapy may require exceptionally precise regulation of P0 expression in human nerve, as only 60% overexpression in mice results in impaired myelin formation.

relevance_reason: Reports an MPZ T124K substitution in a patient with congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy, found by screening MPZ in patients with CMT1, CMT2 and CHN.

findings.statement: Nowakowski and Kochański (2004) screened the MPZ coding and promoter sequences in patients with CMT1, CMT2 and congenital hypomyelinating neuropathy (CHN), using SSCP and heteroduplex analysis. They found a T124K substitution in MPZ in 1 patient with CHN.
quotes: we aimed to analyze the coding and promoter sequences of the MPZ gene in a group of patients with three CMT phenotypes i.e.: CMT1, CMT2 and CHN
in one CHN patient the T124K substitution was detected

findings.statement: Nowakowski and Kochański (2004) found the E56K mutation in MPZ in 1 family with axonal CMT (CMT2). They concluded that MPZ screening should be done across a wide range of CMT phenotypes.
quotes: In one CMT2 family we founded the E56K mutation in the MPZ gene
we conclude that MPZ gene screening should be performed for wide phenotype spectrum of CMT
